newsitem.title: USA: AFL-CIO vows to turn up heat on Yale.
newsitem.headline: AFL-CIO vows to turn up heat on Yale.

text.p: The country's biggest labour organisation vowed Wednesday to step up pressure on Yale University to settle a protracted contract dispute with two of the school's unions.
"We are going to throw the full weight of the federation behind this fight -- this is not a local fight," AFL-CIO spokeswoman Deborah Dion told Reuters by telephone.

Some 312 protesters including AFL-CIO President John Sweeney were arrested in a massive demonstration through New Haven streets Tuesday night. The protesters were charged with creating a public disturbance after they blocked a downtown intersection. All those arrested were later released.

At issue was the Ivy League school's plan to subcontract some service and maintenance jobs on a limited basis. The unions fear letting Yale get its foot in the subcontracting door would result in layoffs and downsizing.
The 295-year-old institution has 10,000 employees, of which 3,700 are unionized under the AFL-CIO umbrella.

The AFL-CIO, with more than 13 million members nationwide, was mulling its next move, Dion said. "The school has broken labour laws," she said. "We can put pressure on the Board of Trustees or we can go to the National Labour Board."
The two Yale unions have been working without contracts since February of this year. Dion said Yale's position was "ludicrous" in light of its $4.8 billion endowment.
"They're making millions of dollars a day just on interest on their endowments. It's just amazing to us that they're going to strip some poor food-service worker out of a job."

Yale says it has offered a 10-year job guarantee to union members and has promised no layoffs as a result of subcontracting, ensuring that the affected union would never shrink below 80 percent of its current size.
"Our objectives are honourable and our proposals are reasonable," Yale spokesman Tom Conroy told Reuters.
The two sides have not held talks since Sept. 10 and no new negotiations are scheduled, Conroy said.
